title: Service stability sprint scenarios + failure model lab
body:
Purpose:
This doc scopes a focused 6-week cross-functional sprint (plus a subsequent 2-week experiment window) to: (a) validate our SLOs and escalation cadence under realistic failure modes, (b) run a small failure-model lab that exercises routing/fallbacks and cache warm/cold behavior, and (c) produce concrete mitigations and playbook changes for product teams and oncall. The emphasis is operational: short feedback loops, measurable experiments, and low blast radius.

Scope and success criteria:
- Scope: production-like staging clusters, subset of customer routes (chat/generation + embeddings), core infra (autoscaler, routing, KV cache), and observability (traces, synthetic checks).
- Success criteria (end of run):
  - Measured error-budget-impact models for 3 failure scenarios with reproducible runbooks.
  - Updated SLO thresholds and alert runbooks or justification for leaving SLOs unchanged.
  - One prioritized mitigation implemented as a canary (eg. routing tweak, cache prewarm hook).
  - Postmortem-style notes for each experiment, containing latency histograms, p95/p99 deviations, and root-cause hypothesis.

Stakeholders and roles (high level):
- Eng SRE (lead): Micah Chen — experiment coordination, hypothesis logging, postmortem drafts.
- Serving Runtime: Riley Patel, Jonah Reed — implement fault injection hooks, model fallback knobs, perf counters.
- Observability: Priya Kaur — synthetic checks, dashboards, traces instrument changes, alert tuning.
- Platform/Infra: Leila Ortiz — create isolated staging environment, node eviction scripts, control autoscaler.
- Product (hosted API): Nora Singh — specify customer routes, acceptance criteria for user-visible regressions.
- Solutions Eng / Customer Success: Aaron Blake — coordinate any customer-impact simulations, review messaging.

High-level timeline (6 + 2 weeks):
- Week 0 (prework, 1 week): environment prep, experiment plan signoff, safety checklist, Github + Jira tickets opened.
- Weeks 1–4 (iterative sprints, two-week cadence): implement hooks, run dry-runs in internal staging, instrument dashboards, run 1st wave experiments.
- Week 5 (analysis & mitigation implementation): triage findings, land quick mitigations, prepare canary.
- Week 6 (canary + review): roll canary to limited traffic, validate metrics, update runbooks.
- Weeks 7–8 (failure-model lab window): more aggressive scenarios with controlled blast radius, full writeups, and final recommendations.

Experiment suite (initial 6 experiments):
1) KV cache cold-start surge
   - Hypothesis: Cold cache on traffic burst increases p99 token latency > SLO for generation routes.
   - Method: Clear KV cache on subset of nodes, generate synthetic traffic with realistic prompt lengths, observe p50/p95/p99.
   - Metrics: p99 generation latency, token output throughput, error rate, CPU/GPU utilization.
   - Safety: limited to staging; throttle client generator.

2) Model-fallback chain validation
   - Hypothesis: Automatic fallback to smaller/quantized model increases latency but preserves availability; fallback may increase failure rates due to input incompatibilities.
   - Method: Inject model-serving failures and trigger routing policy to fallback tier; validate structured output and function-calling behavior.
   - Metrics: availability by route, correctness sampling (automated unit prompts), rollback time.

3) Node eviction + autoscaler race
   - Hypothesis: Aggressive node termination causes transient increased tail latency due to re-sharding and KV rehydration.
   - Method: Simulate node termination events under varying autoscaler settings; track request queueing and dropped requests.
   - Metrics: request queue length, tail latencies, error budget burn.

4) Gradual CPU/GPU throttling
   - Hypothesis: GPU TDP throttles or noisy neighbors cause increased token latency variance; small models more affected by CPU scheduling.
   - Method: Use cgroups to limit CPU/GPU for a set of pods; run mixed workload.
   - Metrics: GPU utilization, token generation time distribution, percent of time grid fails SLO.

5) Synthetic traffic spike with long-context prompts
   - Hypothesis: Long-context prompts exacerbate kernel selection edge-cases causing amplified latency at higher sequence lengths.
   - Method: Synthetic clients generate long-context requests; compare kernel selection logs and fallback counts.
   - Metrics: per-sequence-length latency curves, kernel-switch frequency, memory pressure events.

6) Observability degradation scenario
   - Hypothesis: Missing traces or delayed metrics can mask SLO violations and delay oncall response.
   - Method: Introduce delay in metric exporting or drop a subset of spans; run synthetic checks and measure alerting latency.
   - Metrics: alert time-to-fire, mean time to acknowledge (MTTA), correlation with QA process.

Experiment execution playbook (short):
- Pre-check: confirm staging mirrors production config for routing, models, and KV cache keys; take snapshots of dashboards.
- Run: one experiment owner, one observer (notes), one rollback owner. Log start/stop times to JIRA ticket.
- Post-run: immediate short blameless writeup (< 2 hours), attach logs + traces to ticket, preliminary hypothesis.

Communication and escalation plan:
- Internal: #sre-experiments Slack channel for live updates; pager duty only for real-prod impact (we will not touch prod during lab unless explicitly approved).
- Weekly sync: sprint demo on Fridays with live dashboards and top 3 findings.
- Customer messaging: Solutions Eng will draft any required customer-facing notes if we validate user-visible regressions.

Instrumentation & dashboards to add (observability owner):
- SLO burn rate dashboard per route (generation, chat, embeddings).
- Failure model comparison page showing baseline vs experiment run.
- Alert fatigue tracker (count of noisy alerts during experiments).

Mitigations and quick wins we expect to try:
- Improve prefix/KV prewarm heuristics for high-traffic routes.
- Introduce circuit-breaker thresholds for model fallback to avoid cascading fallbacks.
- Tune autoscaler cool-downs to avoid thrashing during eviction storms.

Risks and safety mitigations:
- Risk: accidental prod impact. Mitigation: experiments limited to staging unless explicit exec approval, kill-switch webhook for all experiments.
- Risk: false positives from synthetic clients. Mitigation: include real traffic sampling when validating final mitigations and use canary.

Acceptance criteria for final recommendations:
- For each failure scenario: clear measurement of SLO impact, at least one proposed mitigation, cost/complexity estimate for mitigation, and PR or ticket to implement.
- SLO adjustments (if any) must include customer impact justification and product signoff.

Open questions / notes to self:
- What is the safe traffic volume limit for staging to model production behavior? (action: ask Leila to provide staging capacity numbers).
- Need to decide canonical list of customer routes for experiments — Nora to finalize by start-of-week-0.
- Are there existing synthetic clients we can reuse for long-context prompts? (Aaron to check).

Next immediate actions (this week):
- Create JIRA epic REL-EXP-2026-09 and tickets for each experiment (Micah).
- Obs to sketch initial dashboards and share JSON (Priya).
- Serving runtime to add a basic fault-injection toggle behind a feature flag (Riley).

Attachments / references:
- https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/Service+Stability+Lab
- JIRA-REL-4512 (environment prep)
- github: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1428 (example instrumentation PR)

If this looks good, I'll open the epic and schedule the prework sync next Tue.

-- Micah
